title: New Scientist Story Ideas — Neuroimaging — September 2026

studies.title: People who donate a kidney to a stranger show a reversed brain map of social closeness
studies.ns_score_reason: a rare, genuinely surprising fMRI result in a hard-to-recruit population, with a matched control group and a clean replication of the standard pattern built in.
studies.the_study: Researchers scanned "extraordinary altruists" — people who had donated a kidney or liver lobe to an anonymous stranger — alongside demographically matched controls, while participants thought about named individuals drawn from different layers of their own social networks. In controls, 75 percent of the brain volume sensitive to social distance responded most strongly to the innermost circle, replicating earlier work. In altruists the pattern flipped: only 30 percent favored the closest circle, and 70 percent responded more strongly to distant acquaintances, with the effect concentrated in the temporoparietal junction.
studies.why_it_matters: The brain's apparent bias toward close kin and friends has been treated as a near-universal feature of human social cognition; this suggests it is at least partly a dimension on which people differ, and that unusually expansive care has a measurable neural signature.
studies.pitch_angle: Open on a donor lying in a scanner thinking about the stranger who received their kidney — and the finding that their brain treats that stranger roughly as most of us treat a sibling. The hook is the reversal of a pattern that has been reported as if it were fixed human nature. Call Shahar Arzy's Computational Neuropsychiatry Lab at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, and it would be worth pairing with Abigail Marsh's long-running work on altruistic donors for an outside view on whether the brain difference is cause, consequence or both.
studies.wider_angle: A longer feature on the science of moral circle expansion — how psychologists and effective-altruism researchers have tried to measure who counts as "one of us", and what happens when the boundary dissolves. Fits a general-interest magazine such as *The Atlantic* or *Aeon*, framed around the ethics of screening donors rather than the imaging.
studies.caveats: Sample size not reported in the abstract and is almost certainly small; cross-sectional design cannot say whether the neural pattern preceded the donation or followed it; fMRI group differences in percentage-of-voxels metrics are sensitive to thresholding choices.

studies.title: A brain marker for loneliness shows up across depression, schizophrenia and Alzheimer's
studies.ns_score_reason: a deliberate replication attempt that succeeded on one measure and failed on another, which is unusually informative; limited by modest per-group numbers.
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Using resting-state and task fMRI in an overlapping cohort (N=167 and N=152; schizophrenia, major depression, Alzheimer's disease and healthy controls), plus mega-analyses combining these with an earlier independent sample (N=317 and N=291), the team tested whether social dysfunction tracks default mode network integrity. Reduced connectivity within the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex was associated with higher social dysfunction and loneliness scores across all groups, and the association extended to depression for the first time. The previously reported link between social dysfunction and default mode responses to emotional faces did not replicate.
studies.why_it_matters: It supports the idea that loneliness and social withdrawal have a shared neural correlate that cuts across diagnostic labels — and simultaneously retires a candidate biomarker that looked promising.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the double result: one brain signature of social withdrawal survives replication, another doesn't. The scenario is a clinic where "withdrawn" means the same thing whether the patient has schizophrenia at 25 or Alzheimer's at 75. Call Simone Braak or Martien Kas (University of Groningen), who led the PRISM consortium work. Avoid implying this is anywhere near a diagnostic test.
studies.wider_angle: A piece on the replication crisis inside psychiatric neuroimaging specifically — why the field is now designing studies whose primary job is to check earlier ones, and what fraction survive. Good for a specialist outlet such as *Nature Medicine*'s news pages or *Undark*.
studies.caveats: Observational; per-diagnosis subgroups are small (26–44); social dysfunction is self-reported; several authors have pharmaceutical industry ties (P1vital Ltd, Boehringer Ingelheim) and one industry-affiliated co-author is an employee of P1vital Products Ltd.

studies.title: People with epilepsy in rural China are now dying of strokes and heart disease, not accidents
studies.ns_score_reason: very large cohort and a clear reversal of the accepted picture, though the setting limits how far readers will see themselves in it.
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: A nationwide cohort followed 17,515 people with epilepsy in rural China for 25,922 person-years (2018–2020), recording 381 deaths. All-cause mortality was 3.5 times the general population rate. Nearly half of deaths were from circulatory disease — cerebrovascular disease 28.9 percent, heart disease 18.9 percent — rather than the drownings, burns and injuries that dominated earlier studies in low-resource settings. The largest relative excess was for brain malignancies (SMR 20.3), pointing to undiagnosed structural lesions.
studies.why_it_matters: It shifts the prevention target for millions of people with epilepsy in low- and middle-income settings from seizure safety toward vascular risk and access to brain scans.
studies.pitch_angle: The surprise is that a historically "accidental" cause-of-death profile has quietly turned into a cardiovascular one as rural China's health profile changed — and that a twentyfold excess of brain tumor deaths implies scans that were never done. Open on the diagnostic pathway: a first seizure in a village clinic with no MRI within reach. Call Ley Liu or Dong Zhou at West China Hospital, or Josemir Sander at UCL's Queen Square Institute of Neurology for international context.
studies.wider_angle: A global health feature on the "imaging gap" — how many neurological diagnoses worldwide depend on a machine most of the planet cannot access, and what portable low-field MRI might change. Fits *The Lancet*'s news pages, *BMJ*, or a development-focused outlet.
studies.caveats: Observational; causes of death partly derived from registry and program records rather than autopsy; three-year follow-up; findings specific to rural China and may not generalize.

studies.title: Sleep apnea leaves a fingerprint in the fine wiring of grey matter
studies.ns_score_reason: a genuinely new imaging window onto a very common condition, held back by small groups and a purely correlational design.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Researchers applied neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI) — a multi-shell diffusion MRI technique that estimates the density and directional spread of neuronal processes — to people with mild (n=24), moderate (n=26) and severe (n=23) obstructive sleep apnea and 24 healthy controls. Widespread changes appeared across grey matter, with orientation dispersion altered more extensively than neurite density, and both increases and decreases depending on region and severity.
studies.why_it_matters: Conventional MRI shows that sleep apnea shrinks brain tissue; this suggests the underlying cytoarchitecture is being reorganized rather than simply lost, which may matter for whether the changes are reversible with treatment.
studies.pitch_angle: Around a billion people have obstructive sleep apnea and most are undiagnosed — the hook is that a technique designed to count neurites can see something in their grey matter that standard scans miss, and that the changes go in both directions rather than simply downward. Open on someone whose partner noticed the snoring. Contact Yun-Zhi Lin at the Second Affiliated Hospital of Dalian Medical University. Do not imply the brain changes cause the daytime cognitive problems — this study cannot show that.
studies.wider_angle: A technical explainer for a neuroscience-literate audience on what NODDI and related diffusion models actually measure and how confidently, given persistent disputes about whether "neurite density index" means what its name implies. Fits a specialist outlet such as *Quanta* or a scientific society magazine.
studies.caveats: Small N in every group (23–26); single-center; cross-sectional and observational; no treatment arm, so nothing can be said about whether CPAP reverses the pattern; multiple-comparison burden is high in whole-brain grey matter statistics.

studies.title: Bilingual children's brains predict the next word in the language they don't learn at school
studies.ns_score_reason: a solid, decently sized first demonstration in an understudied group, but the headline finding is a feasibility result and the individual-differences analyses came out null.
studies.the_study: Eighty-eight Spanish-English bilingual children aged 7–12 listened to a naturalistic story in Spanish, their heritage language, while fNIRS recorded brain activity. The team used a computational language model to estimate how surprising each word was, then tested whether brain responses tracked that surprisal. They did — indicating the children hold rich predictive representations of Spanish. Attempts to link the strength of that tracking to reading and listening comprehension scores in either language produced only trends the authors say are too weak to interpret.
studies.why_it_matters: Heritage languages are routinely treated as weak or incomplete; this shows children's brains are doing the same predictive work in Spanish that monolingual brains do in English, which is relevant to how bilingual children are assessed in schools.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the deficit framing being wrong — a child who seems hesitant speaking Spanish to a teacher is, in the scanner, predicting upcoming Spanish words as fluently as any listener. The methodological hook is that a large language model is being used as a measuring instrument for a child's brain. Call Ioulia Kovelman (now University of Texas at Dallas) or Jonathan Brennan (University of Michigan).
studies.wider_angle: A trend piece on language models as a tool rather than a subject — how surprisal estimates from GPT-style systems have quietly become the standard yardstick in neurolinguistics, and what it means that our theory of human prediction now depends on a commercial artifact. Fits a technology or ideas outlet.
studies.caveats: fNIRS measures only cortical surface hemodynamics, with limited spatial coverage; the individual-differences results were null and the authors say so; no monolingual comparison group; two authors receive royalties from Brookes on Spanish-English assessment instruments (BESA/BESAME).

studies.title: Brain scans of "digital addiction" converge on the same three regions — and on serotonin
studies.ns_score_reason: imposes order on a famously messy literature and links it to chemistry and gene expression, but it is a meta-analysis of heterogeneous, mostly small studies.
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: A voxel-based morphometry meta-analysis pooled structural MRI studies comparing people with problematic social media, gaming or smartphone use against controls. Consistent grey matter reductions emerged in the bilateral anterior cingulate cortex, left middle frontal gyrus and left medial orbitofrontal cortex. Cross-referencing those maps against normative neurotransmitter atlases implicated serotonergic and GABAergic systems rather than the dopamine story usually told about screens, and transcriptomic decoding identified 534 associated genes enriched for synaptic and ion-channel function.
studies.why_it_matters: If it holds, the neurochemistry of compulsive screen use looks less like the stimulant-reward caricature and more like a problem of inhibitory control — which points at different treatments.
studies.pitch_angle: The counterintuitive line is "it's probably not dopamine." Every popular account of phone addiction invokes dopamine hits; the converging imaging evidence points instead at serotonin and GABA systems in regions governing self-control. Open on the gap between the neuroscience and the bestseller shelf. Call Haibo Yang at Tianjin Normal University. Be explicit that grey matter differences in cross-sectional studies cannot say whether heavy use shrank these regions or smaller regions predisposed to heavy use.
studies.wider_angle: An investigation into whether "digital addiction" should be a diagnosis at all — the contested status of internet gaming disorder in DSM-5 and ICD-11, and what happens to a construct when neuroimaging arrives before the definition settles. Fits a psychiatry-focused or long-form outlet.
studies.caveats: Meta-analysis of small primary studies with inconsistent inclusion criteria; cross-sectional throughout, so direction of causation is unknown; "digital addiction" pools several behaviors that may not belong together; neurotransmitter and gene-expression maps come from separate reference cohorts, not the participants themselves.

studies.title: In frontotemporal dementia, poor memory scores don't mean a damaged memory system
studies.ns_score_reason: a clinically useful dissociation with a decent sample, but the framing is technical and the design is cross-sectional.
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Three hundred participants — people with behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia, Alzheimer's disease, mild cognitive impairment, and controls — completed memory tests and had medial temporal lobe volumes measured. Memory scores correlated strongly with medial temporal volume in MCI, moderately in Alzheimer's and controls, and not at all in bvFTD. Propensity score matching showed that once frontal function was accounted for, many apparent memory differences between groups vanished.
studies.why_it_matters: People with bvFTD can fail memory tests while their memory architecture is relatively intact — the failure is in the frontal systems that organize retrieval, which has direct implications for how dementias are told apart in clinic.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is a familiar anxiety inverted: failing a memory test doesn't necessarily mean your memory is broken. Open on a patient in their fifties misdiagnosed with early Alzheimer's on the strength of a word-list score. Call Isabel Santana or Ricardo Félix Morais at the University of Coimbra. Useful for readers who have taken or administered these exact tests.
studies.wider_angle: A feature on the limits of standardized cognitive testing — how tests designed to isolate one faculty end up measuring several, and the push toward test batteries that report *why* someone failed rather than that they did. Fits a psychology or clinical-practice outlet.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional and observational; groups drawn from specialist memory clinics and may not generalize; bvFTD subgroup size not stated separately in the abstract; propensity score matching reduces effective sample size and cannot fully remove confounding.

studies.title: Your brain treats "will they cheat me?" completely differently from "could I lose?"
studies.ns_score_reason: an elegant dissociation, including a brain signal with no behavioral counterpart, but N=31 is thin for parametric fMRI.
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Thirty-one participants played a parametric trust game in an fMRI scanner while three factors varied independently: how much they personally stood to lose, how much their partner stood to gain by betraying them, and whether any betrayal would be deliberate. Behaviorally, people responded almost entirely to their own risk and largely ignored the partner's incentive or agency. Neurally, all three were encoded separately — including partner agency in dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, despite having no effect on choices at all.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests the brain tracks information about a partner's motives that people then fail to use, which is a specific account of why trust decisions are so self-centered.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the mismatch — your brain registers whether someone has a reason to betray you, and then you decide as if it hadn't. Open on a concrete case: handing a deposit to a contractor, or lending money to a colleague. Call Frank Krueger (George Mason University/University of Mannheim), who has built much of this literature. Frame it as a puzzle about information that reaches the brain but not the decision.
studies.wider_angle: A behavioral-economics piece on why trust research keeps finding that people use crude self-focused heuristics, and what that predicts for online marketplaces, escrow design and fraud. Fits a business or economics outlet.
studies.caveats: Small N (31); single-center; lab-based economic game with hypothetical or modest stakes may not reflect real trust decisions; a null behavioral effect paired with a significant neural effect needs independent replication before much weight is put on it.

studies.title: A model using genes, autism and EEG predicts which delayed children will have intellectual disability
studies.ns_score_reason: very large cohort and honest reporting of moderate performance, but the referral-skewed sample and retrospective design cap it.
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Researchers retrospectively analyzed 2,453 children diagnosed with global developmental delay at a Chinese tertiary center between 2014 and 2023, all followed to at least age five, testing 28 candidate predictors spanning perinatal, developmental, neuroimaging, EEG, genetic and comorbidity data across five machine learning algorithms. A calibrated logistic regression achieved an AUC of 0.783 — and, notably, beat nothing: all five algorithms, including gradient boosting and random forests, landed within a 0.015 AUC band of each other. The strongest predictors were pathogenic genetic variants, comorbid autism and epileptiform EEG discharges; a higher adaptive developmental quotient was protective.
studies.why_it_matters: For parents told their toddler is "delayed", the question is always what happens next; this is the first multivariable, calibrated attempt to answer it — and a reminder that fancy algorithms often add nothing over plain regression.
studies.pitch_angle: Two hooks in one: a genuinely useful prognostic tool for a conversation clinicians currently have to hedge, and the quiet embarrassment that four machine learning methods couldn't beat logistic regression. Open in the consulting room at the moment of the "we'll have to wait and see" answer. Contact the corresponding group at the Third Affiliated Hospital of Zhengzhou University. Stress that this is a triage tool for a high-risk referral population, not a community screening test — the authors say so themselves.
studies.wider_angle: A piece on the AI-in-medicine reality check: how often deep and ensemble models are outperformed or matched by simple regressions on tabular clinical data, and why the field keeps rediscovering this. Fits a health-tech or data-science outlet.
studies.caveats: Retrospective and single-center; 83 percent of the cohort progressed to intellectual disability, reflecting extreme referral bias, so the model would need refitting for community use; no external validation; negative predictive value is only 31.7 percent at the chosen threshold.

studies.title: Learning a language in later life helps — but only a narrow slice of thinking
studies.ns_score_reason: deflates a popular claim with a quantitative synthesis, but it is a review with a framework attached rather than new primary data.
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: A review with an embedded quantitative synthesis of behavioral studies in which older adults took up a new language, alongside neuroimaging evidence on which systems late learning recruits. The pooled behavioral effect was small but reliable, and confined largely to higher-order executive processes — attentional regulation, executive coordination, working memory — with no broad enhancement of general cognitive function. Imaging shows engagement of frontal-parietal and memory networks, modulated by task demands and learning stage.
studies.why_it_matters: "Learn a language to protect your brain" is one of the most repeated pieces of cognitive-aging advice; the honest version is narrower and smaller than the slogan.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead with the deflation — yes, it does something, and here is exactly how little and where. Open on a retiree six months into Duolingo streaks wanting to know what they are actually buying. Call Yan Jing Wu at Jiangsu Normal University or the Centre for Cognitive and Brain Sciences at the University of Macau. Be careful not to overstate: this synthesizes existing, mostly small training studies.
studies.wider_angle: An examination of the "cognitive reserve" industry — language apps, brain-training games and puzzle books that borrow scientific credibility from effects this modest, and what the regulatory position on such claims actually is. Fits a consumer-affairs or business outlet.
studies.caveats: Review and secondary synthesis rather than new data; primary training studies are typically small, short and unblinded; publication bias is likely in this literature; no long-term dementia outcomes.

studies.title: Schizophrenia's motivation symptoms track how rigidly the cortex is linked together
studies.ns_score_reason: a reasonable multi-site sample and a specific dissociation, but the effect is small and the concept is hard to translate for general readers.
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Using cortical thickness data from 203 people with schizophrenia across three independent sites, normalized against ENIGMA Lifespan Working Group normative models, the team built structural covariance networks for regions associated with two clusters of negative symptoms: diminished motivation and pleasure (MAP), and diminished expressivity (EXP). Severity of motivation and pleasure deficits predicted how tightly embedded regions were within the MAP network; expressivity deficits showed no such relationship.
studies.why_it_matters: Negative symptoms respond poorly to existing drugs and have long been treated as one thing; this suggests their two components have different neural bases, with apathy tied to excessive structural coupling rather than to loss of tissue in any one region.
studies.pitch_angle: The surprise is that apathy in schizophrenia looks less like a damaged region and more like a network that has become too tightly wired — rigidity rather than deficit. Open on the symptom clinicians find hardest to treat and families find hardest to understand. Call Derin Cobia at Brigham Young University. Frame carefully: this is a correlational imaging association, not a treatment target yet.
studies.wider_angle: A piece on normative modeling — the shift in psychiatric imaging from "patients versus controls" to growth-chart-style deviation scores, and what it lets researchers ask that group averages never could. Fits a specialist neuroscience or psychiatry outlet.
studies.caveats: Observational; the significant effect is small (β=0.085, p=0.03) and would not survive stringent correction across many tests; data pooled from three sites with different scanners; medication effects on cortical thickness not addressed in the abstract; NIH, DOE and NSF funding declared.

studies.title: The cerebellum turns up as an unexpected marker of problem gaming
studies.ns_score_reason: large sample and an unexpected region, but classification accuracy of 62.6 percent is barely above chance and undercuts the biomarker framing.
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: A graph convolutional network was trained on whole-brain functional connectivity graphs from 784 young adults aged 17–32 (453 with internet gaming disorder, 331 controls), with explainability methods used to identify which regions drove the classification. The network beat a linear support vector machine (balanced accuracy 62.6 percent versus 57.7 percent), and both approaches converged on the cerebellum rather than the reward regions usually invoked. Nodal efficiency in cerebellar lobule X, vermal lobule IX and left thalamus correlated negatively with DSM-5 symptom severity — but no correlations with Internet Addiction Test scores survived correction.
studies.why_it_matters: It nudges attention toward the cerebellum's role in habit and compulsion, a region largely absent from the reward-circuit story of behavioral addiction. As a diagnostic tool it is nowhere near useful.
studies.pitch_angle: The cerebellum has spent a century labelled the movement coordinator; here it comes out as the most discriminative region in a large gaming-disorder classifier. Open on the historical dismissal of the "little brain" and the steady accumulation of evidence that it is doing cognitive work. Call Guang-Heng Dong at Yunnan Normal University. Be blunt about the 62 percent accuracy — this is a clue, not a test.
studies.wider_angle: A feature on explainable AI in brain imaging: the field is racing to build classifiers that can say *why*, but saliency maps have known instability problems. Ask whether "the algorithm says cerebellum" is evidence at all. Fits a machine-learning or research-methods outlet.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional; barely-above-chance discrimination; one of two symptom measures produced no surviving correlations, suggesting fragility; attribution methods like CAM and Grad-CAM are not validated as neuroscientific evidence; recruitment restricted to young Chinese adults.

studies.title: Mitochondria may shape how fast time feels — but the evidence is thin
studies.ns_score_reason: an irresistible question and a genuinely unusual patient group, but the authors themselves describe the evidence as weak and the headline group comparison was null.
studies.ns_check: Not verified — SerpAPI unavailable this run
studies.the_study: Sixty-five healthy adults (n=59) and 36 people carrying rare mitochondrial DNA mutations completed time estimation and time production tasks while researchers measured immune-cell mitochondrial bioenergetics, blood and urine catecholamines, resting energy expenditure, working memory, mood and structural and functional MRI. People with mitochondrial disorders did not differ from healthy controls in time perception. However, the *pattern* of associations between time perception and physiological and neural variables differed between the groups, suggesting mitochondrial function moderates which processes shape subjective time.
studies.why_it_matters: Not much yet — but it is the first attempt to connect cellular energy metabolism to the subjective speed of time in humans, and it opens a line of enquiry that has previously been almost entirely theoretical.
studies.pitch_angle: The hook is the question, honestly reported: does the internal clock run on cellular energy? Open on the near-universal experience of time speeding up with age and the fact that nobody can say why. Call Martin Picard at Columbia, whose lab has built its reputation on linking mitochondrial biology to psychological states, and lead with the null — the mutation carriers' time sense was normal. The story must be framed as an exploratory first pass, not a finding.
studies.wider_angle: A feature on mitochondria's expanding portfolio — from energy plants to signaling hubs implicated in stress, mood and aging — and how much of that expansion is supported by evidence. Fits a biology-focused magazine or a critical long-read.
studies.caveats: Exploratory with many measures and weak associations, acknowledged by the authors; small N per group; primary group comparison was null; cross-sectional; findings are hypothesis-generating only.

studies.title: A genetic epilepsy comes with a second kind of seizure that scans can't see
studies.ns_score_reason: the first systematic description of a clinically consequential overlap, but tiny N and retrospective chart review.
studies.ns_check: No recent NS.com coverage found ✓ (0 hits)
studies.the_study: Across six European epilepsy centers, researchers reviewed 27 people with genetically confirmed PCDH19-clustering epilepsy and found that eight (29.6 percent) also had functional, or dissociative, seizures — episodes that look like seizures but produce no epileptic activity on EEG. Median onset was age 16. Six of the eight were initially misdiagnosed as having epileptic seizures, leading to escalating antiseizure medication and hospital admissions. After correct diagnosis and multidisciplinary care, all treated individuals improved.
studies.why_it_matters: It documents a specific and preventable harm — people with a confirmed genetic epilepsy being given more drugs for seizures that are not epileptic — and suggests the two conditions are far from mutually exclusive.
studies.pitch_angle: The counterintuitive premise: having a proven genetic epilepsy makes clinicians *less* likely to consider that a given seizure is functional, and that assumption leads to years of unnecessary medication. Open on an adolescent whose drug doses kept climbing. Call Ángel Aledo-Serrano (Neuralma Institute, Madrid) or Rhys Thomas (Newcastle University). The wider point for readers is that "functional" does not mean fake — and that these seizures responded to treatment.
studies.wider_angle: A feature on functional neurological disorder's rehabilitation as a diagnosis: how a condition once dismissed as hysteria has acquired its own imaging literature, positive diagnostic criteria and effective treatments. Fits a health or medical-history outlet.
studies.caveats: Very small N (27 total, 8 with functional seizures); retrospective chart review across six centers with no standardized protocol; tertiary referral centers select for complex cases; no control group; improvement after treatment reported without systematic outcome measures.

trends_raw:
**Convergent findings**
- *Replication is now a design goal, not an afterthought.* The loneliness/default-mode study (PMID 42044556) is explicitly a confirmatory test: dorsomedial prefrontal connectivity survives across schizophrenia, depression and Alzheimer's, while the emotional-faces default-mode effect does not. That is the same self-auditing impulse seen last run in the failed grey-matter neuroprotection replication of Cognitive Enhancement Therapy (PMID 42623965) and the ABCD subtype clustering that largely came up empty (PMID 41989408).
- *Deflating popular neuro-narratives with numbers.* "Learn a language to protect your aging brain" turns out small and confined to executive processes (PMID 42684539), and the screen-addiction meta-analysis points at serotonergic and GABAergic systems rather than dopamine (PMID 42190596). Both echo last run's 1 percent mediation figure for childhood trauma and bipolar brain morphology (PMID 42234441).
- *Transdiagnostic and normative framing keeps gaining ground.* Social withdrawal tracking one network marker across three diagnoses (PMID 42044556) and negative-symptom severity indexed against ENIGMA Lifespan normative models (PMID 42176687) continue the reclassification pressure of the COGDIS-versus-UHR psychosis-risk study (PMID 41823413) and the RDoC-adjacent subtype failure (PMID 41989408).
- *Imaging is escaping the undergraduate participant pool.* Anonymous organ donors (PMID 42667790), Spanish-English heritage-language children (PMID 42667920) and rural Chinese epilepsy cohorts (PMID 42704311) extend last run's coal-miner fNIRS comparison (PMID 42518290).

**Advances**
- The GENFI work on resilience as an active network property (PMID 41277710) used group modeling; the schizophrenia structural covariance study (PMID 42176687) pushes the same normative-deviation approach into symptom dimensions, separating diminished motivation from diminished expressivity.
- Last run flagged mitochondrial and metabolic signatures as spatial overlays in night-shift nurses (PMID 42624217); this run has direct cellular bioenergetics measured in participants alongside MRI and time perception (PMID 42669931) — a real methodological step up, even though the headline group comparison was null.

**Counterpoints**
- Last run's connectome fingerprinting hit 93–99 percent accuracy at identifying individuals (PMID 42527301). This run's graph convolutional network reaches 62.6 percent balanced accuracy at identifying internet gaming disorder (PMID 42727812). Together they make a sharp point: fMRI is excellent at telling people apart and poor at telling disorders apart.
- The previous digest's implicit hope was that functional and connectivity measures would outperform anatomy. The loneliness replication (PMID 42044556) splits that hope down the middle — one functional marker holds, another dies.

**New themes**
- *Access, not analysis.* The rural China epilepsy cohort (PMID 42704311), with a twentyfold excess of brain malignancy deaths implying scans never done, introduces a global imaging-availability angle absent from the previous digest.
- *Misattributed clinical failure.* Poor memory scores in behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia with intact medial temporal structure (PMID 40995692) and functional seizures misread as epileptic in genetically confirmed PCDH19 epilepsy (PMID 42704296) are a new strand.
- *Algorithms audited rather than celebrated.* Logistic regression matching four machine learning methods on developmental delay prognosis (PMID 42634999), and saliency-map attribution being asked whether it counts as evidence at all (PMID 42727812).
feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Several studies in this batch converge on the same uncomfortable point — the standard tests that decide a diagnosis frequently fail for reasons other than the one printed on the test's name. People with bvFTD flunk memory tests while their memory architecture is intact, the failure sitting in frontal retrieval systems (PMID 40995692); people with a confirmed genetic epilepsy have their functional seizures read as epileptic and their drug doses escalated (PMID 42704296); bilingual children who present as weak in their heritage language turn out to be predicting upcoming Spanish words fluently in the scanner (PMID 42667920); and a calibrated prognostic model for developmental delay reports a negative predictive value of just 31.7 percent, meaning most "reassuring" results aren't (PMID 42634999). The loneliness study adds the mirror image: a single neural marker of social withdrawal that ignores diagnostic boundaries altogether (PMID 42044556).

**Why pitch this now:** Cognitive testing is expanding fast — memory clinics, school language assessments, AI-assisted prognostic scoring — and these papers show, with imaging as the independent arbiter, that the score alone routinely misidentifies what is broken, with consequences that include misdiagnosed dementia, escalating antiseizure medication and children misplaced in school support systems.

**Angle:** A reported feature following one test score through several settings — clinic, school, developmental assessment — asking what it was designed to measure, what it actually measures, and what it would take to report *why* someone failed rather than just that they did. For a science-literate general readership with an appetite for how measurement goes wrong in ordinary institutional settings, told through named patients, clinicians and the researchers auditing their own instruments.

**Potential headlines:**
- Brain scans are revealing that clinical tests often fail for the wrong reason
- Failing a memory test doesn't mean your memory is broken
- The score says impaired, the brain says otherwise — and the treatment follows the score

**Potential outlets:**
- **New Scientist Features** — the batch's home section, and the bvFTD dissociation plus the heritage-language result give the feature two vivid, reader-implicating scenes rather than one abstract argument.
- **STAT** — owns the misdiagnosis-and-overtreatment beat; the PCDH19 medication-escalation finding and the 31.7 percent negative predictive value are exactly its kind of clinical-consequence detail.
- **The Guardian science and health desk** — would carry the education strand well, since heritage-language assessment and developmental-delay prognosis both land on families and schools, not just hospitals.
- **Knowable Magazine** — publishes patiently on measurement validity across disciplines, and this pitch is fundamentally about what a psychometric instrument is licensed to conclude.

### Study 1: People who donate a kidney to a stranger show a reversed brain map of social closeness
**PMID:** 42667790 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Core numbers check out: 75 percent of social-circle-sensitive volume favoring the closest circle in controls, 30/70 reversal in altruists, temporoparietal junction as the focus, demographically matched controls, and the absence of a reported N are all accurately conveyed.

**Issue A. Organ type over-specified** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "people who had donated a kidney or liver lobe to an anonymous stranger"
- **Abstract says:** "extraordinary altruists, who had donated a vital organ to an anonymous recipient"
- **Problem:** The abstract says only "a vital organ." Whether liver-lobe donors were included is unverifiable from abstract only, and the headline commits to kidneys specifically.
- **Suggested fix:** "people who had donated a vital organ — such as a kidney — to an anonymous stranger"

**Issue B. "Treats that stranger roughly as most of us treat a sibling"** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the finding that their brain treats that stranger roughly as most of us treat a sibling"
- **Abstract says:** "only 30% of this brain volume preferred the closest circle, while 70% showed stronger responses to more distant social circles… the closest vs. distant response contrast was significantly smaller in extraordinary altruists"
- **Problem:** The data show reduced selectivity for the innermost circle and a majority of voxels favoring distant circles — not that a stranger is processed equivalently to a named close relative. The paper's own title ("A sibling to all") invites this reading, but the pitch should not present it as a measured equivalence.
- **Suggested fix:** "the finding that their brains show markedly less preference for their closest ties, allocating more of the social-distance signal to people further out"

**Issue C. NS fit score of 8 rests on an unreported sample size** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**NS fit:** 8/10"
- **Abstract says:** No N is reported for either group.
- **Problem:** An 8 is defensible only if the sample is adequate; the digest's own caveat concedes it "is almost certainly small," and percentage-of-voxels metrics are threshold-sensitive. A 7+ score on an unknown, probably small fMRI sample needs hedging.
- **Suggested fix:** Score 7/10 pending confirmation of group sizes from the full text.

### Study 2: A brain marker for loneliness shows up across depression, schizophrenia and Alzheimer's
**PMID:** 42044556 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Sample sizes (N=167, N=152; mega-analyses N=317, N=291), subgroup range (26–44), the replicated dmPFC connectivity association, the extension to MDD, the failed replication of the emotional-faces result, and the industry disclosures are all correctly represented.

**Issue A. Author affiliation** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Call Simone Braak or Martien Kas (University of Groningen), who led the PRISM consortium work."
- **Abstract says:** Braak S — "Amsterdam UMC, location Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, Department of Psychiatry"; Kas MJH — "Groningen Institute for Evolutionary Life Sciences, University of Groningen."
- **Problem:** The parenthetical attaches Groningen to both names; Braak is at Amsterdam UMC. The PRISM consortium attribution is also unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** "Call Simone Braak (Amsterdam UMC) or Martien Kas (University of Groningen)."

**Issue B. Social dysfunction and loneliness treated as two outcomes** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "was associated with higher social dysfunction and loneliness scores across all groups"
- **Abstract says:** "higher mean SFS+LON social dysfunction scores"
- **Problem:** The abstract reports a single composite of the Social Functioning Scale and the De Jong-Gierveld Loneliness scale, not two separately tested outcomes. The headline's "brain marker for loneliness" inherits the same slippage.
- **Suggested fix:** "was associated with higher scores on a combined social-functioning-and-loneliness measure across all groups"

### Study 3: People with epilepsy in rural China are now dying of strokes and heart disease, not accidents
**PMID:** 42704311 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Cohort size (17,515), person-years (25,922), 381 deaths, SMR 3.51, circulatory 47.8 percent with cerebrovascular 28.9 percent and heart disease 18.9 percent, and brain malignancy SMR 20.30 are all accurate.

**Issue A. A study co-author pitched as outside commentary** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Call Ley Liu or Dong Zhou at West China Hospital, or Josemir Sander at UCL's Queen Square Institute of Neurology for international context."
- **Abstract says:** Author list includes "Sander JW(1)(8)(9)" with affiliations "Queen Square Institute of Neurology, London, UK" and "Chalfont Centre for Epilepsy."
- **Problem:** Sander is a co-author on this paper. Offering him as a source "for international context" reads as an independent outside voice and would waste a writer's credibility if pitched that way.
- **Suggested fix:** "Call Ley Liu or Dong Zhou at West China Hospital; note that Josemir Sander (Queen Square Institute of Neurology) is a co-author and cannot serve as the independent voice — source that separately."

**Issue B. Author first name not supported** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Call Ley Liu or Dong Zhou at West China Hospital"
- **Abstract says:** "Liu L" (last author), "Zhou D"
- **Problem:** "Ley Liu" is an expansion of "Liu L" that cannot be verified from the abstract; check the full text before printing a name.
- **Suggested fix:** "Call corresponding author L. Liu, or Dong Zhou, at West China Hospital"

**Issue C. Cause-of-death comparison overstated** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "rather than the drownings, burns and injuries that dominated earlier studies in low-resource settings" / headline: "not accidents"
- **Abstract says:** "Earlier studies in resource-limited settings suggested that accidental deaths were the main causes"
- **Problem:** The abstract says "accidental deaths" generically — drownings and burns are not specified — and it does not report what proportion of this cohort's deaths were accidental, so "not accidents" is an inference rather than a reported contrast.
- **Suggested fix:** "rather than the accidental deaths that earlier studies in resource-limited settings identified as the leading cause"; headline: "…are now dying mostly of strokes and heart disease"

### Study 4: Sleep apnea leaves a fingerprint in the fine wiring of grey matter
**PMID:** 42687385 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

Group sizes (24/26/23 plus 24 controls), the NODDI method, ODI changes being more widespread than NDI, and the bidirectional pattern are all accurate, and the pitch explicitly warns against inferring causation for cognitive symptoms.

**Issue A. Causal claim about prior imaging literature** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Conventional MRI shows that sleep apnea shrinks brain tissue"
- **Abstract says:** "cortical structural alterations have been detected via conventional neuroimaging techniques"
- **Problem:** The abstract describes detected structural alterations, not demonstrated tissue shrinkage, and certainly not sleep apnea *causing* it. The sentence sets up the "Why it matters" with a causal premise the cited work doesn't supply.
- **Suggested fix:** "Conventional MRI has detected structural differences in the brains of people with sleep apnea; this suggests the underlying cytoarchitecture differs too, rather than tissue being simply lost"

**Issue B. Prevalence figure not from this study** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Around a billion people have obstructive sleep apnea and most are undiagnosed"
- **Abstract says:** "Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) is a common chronic multisystem disorder"
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only. The billion figure is widely cited from separate epidemiology and needs its own citation in any pitch.
- **Suggested fix:** "OSA is extremely common — [cite Benjafield et al. 2019 for the ~936 million estimate] — and most cases go undiagnosed"

### Study 5: Bilingual children's brains predict the next word in the language they don't learn at school
**PMID:** 42667920 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=88, ages 7–12, Spanish heritage language, fNIRS, the successful surprisal-tracking result, the uninterpretable individual-differences trends, and the Brookes royalty disclosure are all correctly reported.

**Issue A. Comparison to monolingual brains is not in the study** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "this shows children's brains are doing the same predictive work in Spanish that monolingual brains do in English" / "predicting upcoming Spanish words as fluently as any listener"
- **Abstract says:** "The children demonstrated successful neural tracking of word predictability in their heritage language, suggesting they can form rich linguistic representations in Spanish."
- **Problem:** There was no monolingual group and no English condition; no equivalence was tested. The digest's own caveat notes the absence of a monolingual comparison, but the body text and pitch angle assert exactly that comparison, contradicting the caveat.
- **Suggested fix:** "this shows children's brains are doing predictive work in Spanish of the kind documented in majority-language listening — though this study included no monolingual or English comparison"

**Issue B. "Large language model" / GPT framing** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "a large language model is being used as a measuring instrument for a child's brain" / "surprisal estimates from GPT-style systems"
- **Abstract says:** "a novel computational approach to quantifying linguistic predictions"
- **Problem:** The abstract does not name the model or identify it as an LLM. Unverifiable from abstract only — confirm the model class before building the methodological hook on it.
- **Suggested fix:** "a computational language model is being used as a measuring instrument for a child's brain (confirm model type with authors)"

### Study 6: Brain scans of "digital addiction" converge on the same three regions — and on serotonin
**PMID:** 42190596 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

The three GMV-reduction clusters (bilateral ACC, left MFG, left mOFC), the serotonergic/GABAergic spatial correspondence, the 534 genes and their enrichment for synaptic and ion-channel function are all accurate, and the cross-sectional direction-of-causation caveat is well handled.

**Issue A. "It's probably not dopamine" overstates the abstract** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "implicated serotonergic and GABAergic systems rather than the dopamine story usually told about screens" / "The counterintuitive line is 'it's probably not dopamine.'"
- **Abstract says:** "The findings provide convergent evidence for the involvement of serotonergic, inhibitory, and reward-related neurobiological systems"
- **Problem:** The authors explicitly retain reward-related systems in their conclusion. Spatial correspondence with serotonergic and GABAergic maps does not exclude dopaminergic involvement, and the abstract does not frame the result as a rebuttal of dopamine accounts. The pitch angle's whole hook rests on an exclusion the study does not make.
- **Suggested fix:** "implicated serotonergic and GABAergic systems alongside reward-related circuitry, broadening the dopamine-centric story usually told about screens" — and reframe the pitch as "it's not *only* dopamine."

### Study 7: In frontotemporal dementia, poor memory scores don't mean a damaged memory system
**PMID:** 40995692 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=300, the group composition, the correlation gradient (MCI r=−.58 > AD r=−.36 ≈ controls r=−.35 > non-significant bvFTD r=−.21), and the loss of several group differences after propensity score matching are all accurately reported, as is the absence of a stated bvFTD subgroup size.

**Issue A. "Memory architecture relatively intact" goes beyond the data** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "People with bvFTD can fail memory tests while their memory architecture is relatively intact"
- **Abstract says:** "Significant differences in memory tests and MTL volumes followed the pattern: controls > MCI > bvFTD > AD… AD is primarily marked by MTL-related impairments, which are less pronounced in bvFTD."
- **Problem:** bvFTD participants had significantly smaller MTL volumes than controls and MCI — their medial temporal structures were not intact, only less affected than in AD. The absent correlation means MTL volume doesn't explain their memory scores, which is a different claim from structural preservation.
- **Suggested fix:** "In bvFTD, memory scores are not explained by medial temporal lobe volume at all — MTL atrophy is less pronounced than in Alzheimer's, and frontal contributions appear to drive the test failures"

### Study 8: Your brain treats "will they cheat me?" completely differently from "could I lose?"
**PMID:** 42341477 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=31, the parametric trust game, the three manipulated factors, the null behavioral effect of agency, and the dmPFC encoding of agency despite that null are all accurate.

**Issue A. Behavioral effect of temptation misstated** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Behaviorally, people responded almost entirely to their own risk and largely ignored the partner's incentive or agency."
- **Abstract says:** "trust declined with increasing risk and with the risk × temptation interaction, owing to self-centered heuristics, while agency had no reliable effect."
- **Problem:** Partner temptation *did* influence behavior, in interaction with risk. Only agency had no reliable behavioral effect. Lumping temptation in with agency misstates which factor produced the brain-behavior dissociation the whole pitch is built on. The body's "all three were encoded separately" is also loose — temptation was encoded in interaction with risk.
- **Suggested fix:** "Behaviorally, people responded to their own risk and to risk-by-temptation interactions, but a partner's agency had no reliable effect on choices. Neurally, agency was nonetheless distinguished in dorsomedial prefrontal cortex."

**Issue B. Study population and setting not stated** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Thirty-one participants played a parametric trust game in an fMRI scanner" / Caveats: "single-center"
- **Abstract says:** Author affiliations are University of Tehran, Iran University of Medical Sciences, George Mason University and University of Mannheim; the abstract gives no participant demographics or recruitment site.
- **Problem:** The digest asserts a single center without support and omits that the scanning was most likely done in Iran, which is relevant for a study about trust norms. Unverifiable from abstract only.
- **Suggested fix:** Add to Caveats: "Recruitment site and participant demographics are not stated in the abstract; author affiliations suggest data collection in Tehran — confirm before generalizing about 'trust decisions' broadly."

### Study 9: A model using genes, autism and EEG predicts which delayed children will have intellectual disability
**PMID:** 42634999 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=2,453, the 2014–2023 window, minimum follow-up to 60 months, 28 candidate predictors, AUC 0.783, the 0.015 AUC band, the three strongest risk factors, the protective adaptive DQ, the 83.0 percent ID rate, the 31.7 percent NPV and the authors' own triage-not-screening caveat are all accurate.

**Issue A. Miscount of the non-regression algorithms** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the quiet embarrassment that four machine learning methods couldn't beat logistic regression"
- **Abstract says:** "Five algorithms—L2- and L1-regularised logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost and LightGBM"
- **Problem:** Two of the five are logistic regressions. Only three tree-based methods failed to beat the calibrated L2 model, not four.
- **Suggested fix:** "the quiet embarrassment that three tree-based machine learning methods couldn't beat a calibrated logistic regression"

### Study 10: Learning a language in later life helps — but only a narrow slice of thinking
**PMID:** 42684539 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. The "small but reliable" pooled effect, its confinement to higher-order executive processes (executive coordination, attentional regulation, working memory), the explicit absence of broad general-cognition enhancement, the frontal-parietal and memory-network imaging findings, and the review-not-primary-data status are all correctly represented. Author affiliations (Wu at Jiangsu Normal University; Centre for Cognitive and Brain Sciences, University of Macau) check out. Framing is appropriately deflationary and the caveats about small, short, unblinded training studies are consistent with a review-level claim.

### Study 11: Schizophrenia's motivation symptoms track how rigidly the cortex is linked together
**PMID:** 42176687 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. N=203 across three independent sites, the ENIGMA Lifespan normative modeling, the MAP/EXP structural covariance networks, the selective MAP finding (β = 0.085, p = 0.03) with no corresponding EXP effect, and the "over-coupling / network rigidity" interpretation all match the abstract. The NIH/DOE/NSF funding disclosure is carried into Caveats, and the pitch explicitly labels the result correlational and not yet a treatment target. A 4/10 fit score is defensible for a small effect in a technical framework.

### Study 12: The cerebellum turns up as an unexpected marker of problem gaming
**PMID:** 42727812 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

N=784 (453 IGD, 331 controls), ages 17–32, balanced accuracy 62.60 vs 57.65 percent, the convergence of CAM, Grad-CAM and SVM on the cerebellum, and the failure of any IAT correlation to survive correction are all accurate. The "this is a clue, not a test" framing is appropriately blunt.

**Issue A. Lateralization dropped** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Nodal efficiency in cerebellar lobule X, vermal lobule IX and left thalamus correlated negatively with DSM-5 symptom severity"
- **Abstract says:** "nodal efficiency was significantly and negatively correlated with DSM-5 severity in the left cerebellar lobule X, vermal lobule IX, and left thalamus, with a marginally significant correlation in the right hippocampus"
- **Problem:** The cerebellar finding is specifically left lobule X; the digest drops the side. The marginally significant right hippocampus result is also omitted, which matters because the paper's title frames a cerebello-thalamo-hippocampal network.
- **Suggested fix:** "Nodal efficiency in the left cerebellar lobule X, vermal lobule IX and left thalamus correlated negatively with DSM-5 symptom severity, with a marginal effect in the right hippocampus"

### Study 13: Mitochondria may shape how fast time feels — but the evidence is thin
**PMID:** 42669931 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

The task battery, the physiological and neuroimaging measures, the null group comparison, the differential association patterns and the authors' own "weak evidence" characterization are all faithfully reported, and the digest correctly leads with the null.

**Issue A. Contradictory sample size for the healthy group** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Sixty-five healthy adults (n=59) and 36 people carrying rare mitochondrial DNA mutations"
- **Abstract says:** "a cohort of healthy adults (n = 59) and individuals carrying rare mitochondrial DNA mutations affecting mitochondrial energy transformation (n = 36)"
- **Problem:** The sentence gives two different numbers for the same group. "Sixty-five" appears nowhere in the abstract; the healthy group is n = 59 and the total cohort is 95.
- **Suggested fix:** "Fifty-nine healthy adults and 36 people carrying rare mitochondrial DNA mutations"

### Study 14: A genetic epilepsy comes with a second kind of seizure that scans can't see
**PMID:** 42704296 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

27 individuals with genetically confirmed PCDH19-clustering epilepsy, eight (29.6 percent) with functional seizures, median FDS onset at 16, six initially misdiagnosed with consequent ASM escalation and hospitalizations, and improvement in all treated individuals are all accurate. The "functional does not mean fake" framing is well judged and the caveats cover the retrospective, referral-biased design.

**Issue A. Headline says "scans" for an EEG finding** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** Headline: "A genetic epilepsy comes with a second kind of seizure that scans can't see"
- **Abstract says:** Diagnosis was per ILAE criteria using "neurophysiological" among other data; the distinguishing feature of functional seizures is the absence of ictal epileptiform activity on EEG.
- **Problem:** EEG is not a scan, and the study collected neuroimaging data separately. For a neuroimaging-focused digest this risks a reader assuming MRI findings that the abstract does not report.
- **Suggested fix:** "A genetic epilepsy comes with a second kind of seizure that doesn't show up on EEG"

**Issue B. Claim about clinician reasoning not tested** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "having a proven genetic epilepsy makes clinicians *less* likely to consider that a given seizure is functional, and that assumption leads to years of unnecessary medication"
- **Abstract says:** "Six patients were initially misdiagnosed with epileptic seizures, resulting in unnecessary antiseizure medication (ASM) escalation and hospitalizations."
- **Problem:** The abstract documents that misdiagnosis happened in six of eight cases; it does not measure clinician reasoning, compare against a group without a genetic diagnosis, or report duration ("years") of inappropriate treatment.
- **Suggested fix:** "Six of the eight were initially misdiagnosed with epileptic seizures and had their medication escalated — raising the question of whether a confirmed genetic diagnosis makes clinicians less likely to consider a functional cause"
